title: Our Mutual Friend: A Literary Discussion

segments.title: Opening: The Dust Heaps and London's Underworld

utterances.text: Welcome to Our Mutual Friend Unpacked — a close, unhurried look at one of the greatest and most underrated novels in the English language.
Our Mutual Friend was Charles Dickens's last completed novel, published in 1864 and 1865, and it is a book of staggering ambition.
It gives us dust heaps that stand for inherited wealth, a river that carries the dead, a society so obsessed with money it has forgotten what human beings are for.
Over the course of this series, we will move through the novel passage by passage — its comedy, its darkness, its extraordinary prose.
Joining me today are three readers who know this book very well indeed, and who each bring a completely different set of ears to it.
Sir Edmund Leigh is a retired Oxford don and a literary critic of the old school — which is to say, the best school.
Edmund reads novels as stories about individual moral character — about goodness, self-deception, and the tests that circumstance puts to the human will.
Professor James Blackstone is a legal and social historian who specialises in the real institutions that novelists put on the page.
When Dickens draws the workhouse, the law court, or the debtors' prison, James knows exactly what those places were — and what it cost to be inside them.
And Ms Caroline Woodcourt is a book critic who first read Our Mutual Friend as a teenager and has never quite got over it.
Caroline's gift is attending to the experience of reading — the sentence that stops you cold, the character who makes you laugh out loud on the top deck of a bus.
We begin at the beginning — with the novel's world as Dickens first frames it: a London run on dust and pretension, presided over by the river.
What strikes me first, every time, is how immediately Dickens locates the machinery of class — not as background, but as the engine of the comedy itself.
Take the introduction of Twemlow — one of the great comic inventions in the novel.
Dickens presents him not as a man but as a piece of furniture.
He is, in the narrator's words, quote:
"an innocent piece of dinner-furniture that went upon easy castors and was kept over a livery stable-yard in Duke Street, Saint James's, when not in use."
The satire is exquisitely calibrated — Twemlow is aristocratic by connection but entirely without agency.
He is stored, retrieved, and extended according to the Veneerings' social needs — and the more he is extended, the further he finds himself from the centre of the table.
That is a precise description of how the English class system actually worked — and still works, if we're honest about it.
James is quite right about the precision — though I should want to resist the temptation to read the Veneerings purely as indictment.
What Dickens is doing is something more subtle — and more damning — than mere social criticism.
He is showing us what happens to a human being when he accepts the role that society assigns him.
Twemlow consents to being furniture — and that consent is the moral failure Dickens is really interested in.
The line about being first cousin to Lord Snigsworth — that is where the comedy cuts deepest.
The name itself is a verdict.
Dickens always trusted the names to do a great deal of the work — and here they do.
What I love about the Twemlow passage — and I remember this vividly from the first reading — is that the joke compounds itself.
It begins as a clever conceit, and then Dickens just keeps extending it — literally — past all reasonable limits.
Twemlow at twelve leaves, Twemlow at twenty leaves — pulled out to his utmost extent.
And that image of him always ending up nearer to the window-curtains — there's something genuinely melancholy underneath the laughter.
That's what Dickens does constantly in this novel — the comedy and the sadness are the same sentence.
Caroline's point about the comedy-sadness compound matters enormously when we look at some of the other characters in the novel's lower registers.
Take the description of Sloppy in his new black suit — Mrs Boffin's act of kindness that the tailor's craft cannot quite redeem.
The passage tells us that the tailor received personal directions to expend the utmost cunning of his art — specifically to conceal the buttons.
And here is what happened instead:
"he now stood before the Council, a perfect Argus in the way of buttons: shining and winking and gleaming and twinkling out of a hundred of those eyes of bright metal, at the dazzled spectators."
The Argus myth — the hundred-eyed giant — is deployed here with genuine wit: Sloppy's body defeats civilisation's best efforts at concealment.
But what strikes the historian is the context: this is what it looked like when charitable patronage dressed up the poor for polite inspection.
The Argus conceit is wonderfully literary — and I think it does something that mere social observation cannot.
Sloppy's body refuses the grammar of respectability — and this is not merely funny, it is a kind of dignity.
There is a passage shortly after where Dickens piles on the indignities of the hat — the fluted hatband with its black bunch — and the word he uses is magnificent.
He says the imagination shrunk discomfited — as if even the power of fancy recoils.
That is not social criticism — that is a novelist absolutely in command of his comic resources.
I want to turn from comedy to something altogether darker — because this novel contains both, and they are never far apart.
There is a passage describing a train journey through London that I find almost unbearably powerful.
Dickens follows the train as it tears through house-tops and torn-down streets and over the river — and the simile he reaches for is violent and exact.

"the train rattled among the house-tops, and among the ragged sides of houses torn down to make way for it, and over the swarming streets, and under the fruitful earth, until it shot across the river: bursting over the quiet surface like a bomb-shell, and gone again as if it had exploded in the rush of smoke and steam and glare."
A bomb-shell — not a metaphor of progress but of destruction.
And then Dickens turns to Father Time, going straight to his end — and the river running beneath, indifferent, many-sourced, with one sure termination.
It is the most beautiful and terrible compression of the novel's whole theme in a single paragraph.

That passage captures something about industrial London that no social history has quite managed — the sense of violent simultaneity, the old city being demolished as the new one accelerates through it.
And the novel is equally unflinching when it turns to violence of a more personal and premeditated kind.
The confrontation between Riderhood and Bradley Headstone is one of the most disturbing scenes in all of Dickens — and one of the most legally precise.
Riderhood has witnessed everything — the change of clothes, the dip in the river, the discarded bundle — and he recites the evidence with the relish of a man who knows exactly what it is worth.
And then he delivers his verdict in six words that close like a trap:
"I've got your Bargeman's clothes, tore this way and that way with the scuffle, stained green with the grass, and spattered all over with what bust from the blows. I've got them, and I've got you."
That repetition — I've got them, and I've got you — is not rhetoric, it is blackmail reduced to its barest grammar.
And the scene tells us something important: in Dickens's London, the poor watch everything — because watching is the only power they have.
James puts it well — though I should observe that Riderhood is not merely a victim deploying the only weapon available to him.
He is a genuinely malicious creature — and Dickens does not sentimentalise him.
What makes the scene so uncomfortable is that two forms of wickedness face each other — and neither has any claim on our sympathy.
That is a moral complexity that very few novelists are bold enough to sustain.
We have, in the space of a few passages, moved from dinner-furniture to bomb-shells to blackmail — which is, I think, a reasonably accurate summary of what this novel contains.
In our next segment, we turn to the characters at the heart of the novel — to the Wilfer household, to Bella's ambitions, and to the strange courtship at the centre of the plot.
Stay with us.

segments.title: Bella's Reckoning: From Mercenary to Genuine

utterances.text: Welcome back to Our Mutual Friend Unpacked.
We've been tracing the great arcs of moral transformation that run through this novel like veins of gold through dark rock.
This segment turns to perhaps the most contested of those arcs: Bella Wilfer's journey from self-declared mercenary to something altogether more genuine.
Sir Edmund Leigh is here to read the moral landscape with his characteristic precision.
Professor James Blackstone will keep us anchored to the social realities that shape these characters' choices.
And Caroline Woodcourt brings what she always brings: an attention to the sentence-by-sentence experience of reading Dickens aloud.
Edmund, let's begin with you — and with the Boffins, whose own moral simplicity sets the standard against which Bella is measured.
The Boffins are, in one sense, the novel's moral touchstone — and Dickens places them there with characteristic economy.
There is a moment of almost heartbreaking simplicity when Mr Boffin looks at his wife and says what he has said, one imagines, a thousand times before.
'Yes; and it's pleasant to know that you are Mrs Boffin, and it's been a pleasant thing to know this many and many a year!'
Dickens then delivers the satirical sting with perfect control: 'It was ruin to Mrs Boffin's aspirations, but, having so spoken, they sat side by side, a hopelessly Unfashionable pair.'
That capital U in 'Unfashionable' is doing considerable work — Dickens is not merely describing their social position, he is awarding them a distinction.
The people who cannot become fashionable precisely because they are too good — that is Dickens's highest compliment.
Bella must travel a long road before she arrives at that kind of uncomplicated goodness.
And what makes Bella's road so compelling to read is that she knows she is on the wrong one — she admits it, quite cheerfully, at the outset.
She wants money, she says so, and she is not in the least ashamed.
But John Harmon — or rather John Rokesmith, as he presents himself — is watching her with an almost clinical purpose.
He explains quite nakedly in his great confession what the scheme was from the beginning.
'The plot was made out of our getting common sailors' dresses, and throwing ourselves in Bella Wilfer's neighbourhood, and trying to put ourselves in her way.'
There is something both touching and faintly alarming about a man who disguises himself as a common sailor to judge whether the woman he is obliged to marry is worthy of him.
But the novel insists we take it seriously — and eventually we do, because Bella takes it seriously too.
That word 'proving' is worth dwelling on, because Harmon uses it in a very precise sense.
He says he conceived the plan of, in his own phrase, 'proving Bella' — and the verb carries the weight of a legal and moral test simultaneously.
'The thought entered my head of turning the danger I had passed through, to the account of being for some time supposed to have disappeared mysteriously, and of proving Bella.'

The legal resonance matters here — a will has already disposed of Bella as a property, and Harmon is trying to establish whether the woman herself has any independent moral worth beyond that disposition.
The dread he names is equally precise: perpetuating the fate of his father's riches — that they should lead to nothing but evil.
He is not simply testing Bella's affections — he is trying to break a generational curse transmitted by money itself.
Blackstone is right to press on that phrase, and I would add that Dickens's framing here is unusually sympathetic to Harmon's moral timidity.
The novel does not present this deception as a straightforward wrong — it presents it as an act born of a genuinely damaged childhood.
And the test is passed, emphatically, once Bella has encountered genuine poverty and suffering — not the romantic poverty of novels, but the kind that degrades.
Lizzie Hexam's description of that wretched child is not incidental to Bella's arc — it is the catalyst.
'This poor ailing little creature has come to be what she is, surrounded by drunken people from her cradle — if she ever had one, Charley.'
That parenthetical — 'if she ever had one' — is one of those moments where Dickens makes the reader flinch.
It is not sentimental — it is ferocious.
That line always stops me — every time, no matter how often I've read it.
The aside is so quiet, so nearly offhand, and then you sit with it and realise it contains an entire condemned life.
And what Dickens is doing, I think, is using this child's suffering to measure the moral distance Bella still needs to travel.
Bella has been complaining about not being rich enough — and here is what the other end of that spectrum actually looks like.
Dickens never lets the novel's comedy entirely screen out that kind of darkness.
The comedy and the darkness are often in the same breath, actually — nowhere more so than in Boffin's magnificent tirade against charity patrons.
Bella is present for this speech, and it is part of her education — an education in the difference between the performance of virtue and the thing itself.
Boffin names the whole system of titled giving with a kind of exasperated precision that is very funny and absolutely accurate.

'Patrons and Patronesses, and Vice-Patrons and Vice-Patronesses, and Deceased Patrons and Deceased Patronesses, and Ex-Vice-Patrons and Ex-Vice-Patronesses — what does it all mean in the books of the Charities that come pouring in on Rokesmith as he sits among 'em pretty well up to his neck!'
That list — the sheer accumulation of it — is a comic masterpiece, but it is also a precise description of how Victorian philanthropic culture laundered social ambition as benevolence.
Bella is learning, in the Boffin household, that money and moral title do not coincide — and that is the foundation of her transformation.
There is one more passage I want to bring in, because it sits in the darkest corner of this segment and illuminates the rest by contrast.
Bradley Headstone is the novel's portrait of a transformation that goes entirely the wrong way — a man consumed not by money but by passion.
And Dickens renders his deterioration in a passage of extraordinary gothic intensity.

'Rigid before the fire, as if it were a charmed flame that was turning him old, he sat, with the dark lines deepening in his face, its stare becoming more and more haggard, its surface turning whiter and whiter as if it were being overspread with ashes, and the very texture and colour of his hair degenerating.'
That word 'degenerating' — applied to the texture and colour of his hair — is doing something almost biological.
Headstone does not age — he corrodes.
Set him beside the Boffins, sitting side by side in their hopelessly Unfashionable contentment, and you have the novel's moral geometry in miniature.
The contrast really is that stark — and it makes Bella's arc feel all the more urgent.
She could tip either way — and the novel keeps the reader genuinely uncertain for a long time.
What saves her, I think, is that she has a capacity for honest self-examination that Bradley Headstone entirely lacks.
He cannot see what he is becoming — she can, and she chooses differently.
The geometry Edmund described — Boffins versus Headstone, with Bella navigating between — feels like the key to the whole novel's moral argument.
We'll be carrying that thread into our next segment, where we look at how the novel treats money not merely as a theme but as an almost physical force — corrupting, inheriting, transmitting.
Stay with us.

segments.title: The Golden Dustman's Conscience: Wealth and Moral Corruption

utterances.text: Welcome back to Our Mutual Friend Unpacked.
Today we're turning our attention to the question at the moral heart of this novel: what does sudden wealth actually do to a person?
Nicodemus Boffin — the Golden Dustman — inherits a fortune built on refuse, and the world descends on him almost immediately.
With me today are three readers who've spent a great deal of time thinking about this novel from very different angles.
Sir Edmund Leigh brings the perspective of a literary critic who believes great fiction is ultimately about individual character — goodness, weakness, moral imagination.
Professor James Blackstone is a legal and social historian who can tell us what the institutions in this novel actually were, and what they cost real people.
And Caroline Woodcourt is a book critic who has lived with this novel since she was a teenager and cares deeply about what it feels like to read every page.
Let's begin with the flood — the extraordinary deluge of begging letters and charitable solicitations that greets Boffin's new fortune.
What Dickens captures in those chapters is something that had a very precise social reality in the eighteen-sixties.
The explosion of charitable institutions in Victorian England was genuine — and so was their appetite for wealthy patrons of new money.
What Dickens renders with such ferocity is the mechanism: the way notoriety converts a man into a target.
The Secretary opens the letters, and the narration becomes this extraordinary catalogue of organised extraction.
"Oh the varieties of dust for ocular use, offered in exchange for the gold dust of the Golden Dustman!"
That phrase — dust for ocular use — is not merely satirical wit; it is a structural argument about what charity can become.
You are given spectacles of benevolence in exchange for real money.
The duke's letter, lithographed by the hundred, is only the most brazen example.
What strikes me every time I re-read those pages is the sheer comic velocity of it — the list just keeps arriving, wave after wave.
And then it tips quite suddenly into something darker with the individual beggars.
The line about their documents is perfectly cruel and perfectly true.
"They call their scraps documents; but they are, as to papers deserving the name, what minced veal is to a calf."
You laugh — and then you realise you've just laughed at people who are genuinely desperate.
That is Dickens at his most uncomfortable: the comedy and the tragedy are the same sentence.
And poor Boffin — he never quite asked for any of this.
I think one has to be careful not to read Boffin's predicament as purely a social phenomenon.
The begging letters are the occasion; the real question is what Boffin does with the occasion — and what it reveals about him.
What is deeply interesting to me is the will that sets all this in motion.
Wegg reads it aloud with that ghastly buoyancy of his, and the document itself is almost a satire on human connection.
"Inasmuch as he has never made friends, and has ever had a rebellious family, he, John Harmon, gives to Nicodemus Boffin the Little Mound, which is quite enough for him."
"Quite enough for him" — that phrase is extraordinary in its coldness.
Old Harmon does not trust Boffin with great wealth; he parcels it out with a kind of contemptuous frugality.
And yet that is precisely the wealth that transforms Boffin — which raises the question of whether transformation was always latent in the man.
Edmund raises something historically important there.
Old Harmon's will — and the legal machinery around it — is a precise portrait of how Victorian inheritance law worked to concentrate and punish at the same time.
The residue goes to the Crown — which in practice meant a lengthy legal process, Chancery-adjacent, deeply corrosive.
What Dickens understood is that enormous wealth, especially unearned wealth, does not liberate — it places you inside a set of social obligations you cannot refuse.
The Duke of Linseed's lithographed letter makes that perfectly explicit — the fee is three guineas, but the real cost is your dignity.
There's a passage I keep returning to that I think complicates both of those readings rather beautifully.
Eugene Wrayburn, describing his father — he calls him M. R. F., Most Respected Father — with this extraordinary mixture of filial affection and savage comedy.
The passage captures how class and family pre-assign a man's entire identity before he's drawn a breath.
"When my second brother was going to be born by-and-by, 'this,' says M. R. F., 'is a little pillar of the church.' Was born, and became a pillar of the church; a very shaky one."
A very shaky one — I never tire of that.
Eugene describes his own destiny — barrister and married man — with the same tone, as though his entire life were a joke arranged by someone else.
That sense of a life pre-allocated — it isn't so distant from what happens to Boffin, whose wealth is also arranged for him by the dead.
Caroline is quite right to draw that parallel, and I think it illuminates something about the novel's central moral argument.
Eugene's comedy about M. R. F. is also, if one looks carefully, a comedy about the abdication of self-determination.
To be amused by the arrangements made for one is a way of not resisting them.
Now consider what happens on the river — the accusation against Gaffer Hexam.
Riderhood stands up with that cap in his hands and delivers his information with a kind of dreadful ceremony.
"I give information that the man that done the Harmon Murder is Gaffer Hexam, the man that found the body.
The hand of Jesse Hexam, commonly called Gaffer on the river and along shore, is the hand that done that deed. His hand and no other."
That repetition — his hand and no other — is the grammar of false certainty.
Riderhood doesn't know; he swears with the precision of a man performing conviction rather than possessing it.
And that performance — that moral fraud — is not unconnected to the world of the begging letters and the duke's lithographed conscience.
The Riderhood scene is also a legal document of sorts — an information laid before the authorities — and it's worth noting how the novel treats the whole machinery of accusation.
In the eighteen-sixties there was a real culture of informants — people who traded accusations for rewards or to settle scores.
Riderhood uses the formal language of official testimony — he asks to be taken down, as if he were in a magistrate's court.
It's a grotesque appropriation of legal authority by someone who has absolutely none.
And what ties all of this together — the begging letters, the false accusation, Eugene's resigned amusement — is the question of what people do when they want money or power they haven't earned.
That seems to me exactly the thread running through all of this — the novel is obsessed with the gap between what people claim and what they are.
And Boffin sits at the centre of it — a genuinely good man subjected to every form of moral pressure the world can devise.
In our next segment, we'll look more closely at how the novel charts what wealth actually does to Boffin's character — and whether he emerges from it with his soul intact.

segments.title: John Harmon's Shadow: The Man Who Wasn't There

utterances.text: Welcome to Our Mutual Friend Unpacked, the programme that takes Dickens's last completed novel apart, chapter by chapter, and holds the pieces up to the light.
I'm your host, and today we're exploring one of the most daring structural gambits in all of Victorian fiction: the hero who isn't there.
John Harmon — heir, presumed drowned, secret lodger in his own story — haunts every page of this novel like a man reading his own obituary.
To unpack him, I have three exceptional readers with me.
Sir Edmund Leigh is a retired Oxford don whose lifelong conviction is that great novelists live or die by their moral imagination, not their social programme.
Professor James Blackstone brings the historian's eye: what these institutions actually were, what the law meant, what it cost to be poor.
And Caroline Woodcourt is a book critic who first read this novel as a teenager and has never quite recovered — which, if you ask me, is exactly the right response.
Let's begin with the Boffins — because before we can understand what John Harmon means to this novel, we need to understand what the Boffins meant to John Harmon.
The Boffins are, in a sense, the moral centre of gravity in this novel — the fixed point around which all the other characters orbit.
And what Dickens establishes early — through Boffin's own testimony — is that their care for the boy John Harmon was not sentimental, but tested under fire.
Boffin recounts to Mortimer Lightwood the old man's rages — his cruelty to young John — and then there is this extraordinary moment.
"I have seen him, after Mrs Boffin has given him her mind respecting the claims of the nat'ral affections, catch off Mrs Boffin's bonnet and send it spinning across the yard."

"And once, when he did this in a manner that amounted to personal, I should have given him a rattler for himself, if Mrs Boffin hadn't thrown herself betwixt us, and received flush on the temple. Which dropped her, Mr Lightwood. Dropped her."
That repetition — 'Dropped her' — is Dickens at his most precise.
Boffin does not reach for rhetorical elevation. He lands the blow on the listener just as Old Harmon landed it on his wife.
What strikes me every time I re-read that passage is the bonnet.
Dickens gives us that parenthetical — 'she wore, in general, a black straw, perched as a matter of convenience on the top of her head' — and the whole scene becomes visible.
You see the yard. You see the bonnet spinning. And then you see Mrs Boffin fall.
The comic detail and the violent detail occupy exactly the same sentence, which is very Dickens and very disturbing.
But what it also establishes — and this is crucial for John Harmon's arc — is that these two people suffered real cost on his behalf.
His debt to them is not abstract. It is written in Mrs Boffin's bruised temple.
And it is a debt Harmon himself eventually names with remarkable directness.
When he finally confronts Wegg, the mask comes off — and the language he uses about the Boffins is extraordinary.
"I owe everything I possess, solely to the disinterestedness, uprightness, tenderness, goodness — there are no words to satisfy me — of Mr and Mrs Boffin."
'There are no words to satisfy me' — that parenthesis is Harmon confessing the limits of language in the face of genuine virtue.
The legal historian in me notices that Dickens is staging something quite precise here: Harmon's title to the fortune is not ancestral, it is earned — earned by the Boffins' surrender of it.
The Dutch bottle, the conditions, the mound — it is a transfer by gift, not by law.
Dickens is quietly insisting that moral claim and legal claim are two very different things — and that only one of them matters.
Blackstone is right to press on the mechanics of that transfer, and I think it illuminates something about Harmon's disguise that we risk sentimentalising.
The man returns to England to see whether his father's arranged bride is someone he could love — that is, at root, a test of his own will and judgement.
The drowning, the substitution, the false identity — all of it prolongs that test beyond any reasonable limit.
And Dickens himself, in one of his postscripts, confronts this quite candidly.

"I foresaw the likelihood that a class of readers and commentators would suppose that I was at great pains to conceal exactly what I was at great pains to suggest: namely, that Mr John Harmon was not slain, and that Mr John Rokesmith was he."
He is asking for patience — the patience due to a craftsman who knows what he is doing.
Whether one grants that patience depends, I think, on whether one finds the disguise morally interesting or merely convenient.
I find it morally interesting, but I'll confess the disguise also produces something that I find genuinely moving — which is Mrs Boffin's impulse.
Before any of the plot mechanics grind into motion, before Rokesmith appears at the door, Mrs Boffin says something that I think is the emotional key to the whole novel.
"Now that he is past all benefit of the money, and it's come to us, I should like to find some orphan child, and take the boy and adopt him and give him John's name, and provide for him."
She wants to resurrect him in effigy because she cannot resurrect him in fact.
And of course — at that very moment — John Harmon is alive, and listening, and the reader suspects it.
The dramatic irony is almost unbearable. Dickens holds it there without flinching.
That impulse of Mrs Boffin's also has a social dimension worth pausing on.
Adoption in the Victorian sense was not a legal status — it had no formal standing in English law until 1926.
What Mrs Boffin is proposing is an act of pure moral will — taking a child, giving it a name, providing for it — with no legal scaffold whatsoever.
Which rhymes, rather precisely, with the Boffins' broader relationship to the fortune: they hold it on moral terms, not legal ones.
And Dickens consistently sides with the moral claim — which, in 1864, was not the obvious position to take.
We've been circling John Harmon himself — his absence, his debt, the people who kept faith with him.

But there's one more piece of this picture I want to bring in — because Dickens does something rather unusual with the rooftop scenes: he places characters in a garden above the city's grime, and asks us to consider what redemption might actually look like.
Caroline, there's a passage involving Lizzie Hexam and Jenny Wren that I think speaks directly to this question of identity and sanctuary.
Yes — and it's a passage I love partly because it sits so unexpectedly in the middle of all the novel's darkness.
Riah has brought Lizzie and Jenny up to his rooftop garden — this small improbable oasis above the London chimneys.
And Dickens describes the scene with a tenderness that is almost pastoral.

"Lizzie Hexam and Jenny Wren. For whom, perhaps with some old instinct of his race, the gentle Jew had spread a carpet. Seated on it, against no more romantic object than a blackened chimney-stack over which some bumble creeper had been trained, they both pored over one book; both with attentive faces."
'No more romantic object than a blackened chimney-stack' — and yet it is romantic, entirely.
Two women, one book, shared attention — it is one of the quietest images of human dignity in the whole novel.
What Dickens is doing in that scene is building a counter-world — a place where the novel's more battered characters can exist without being defined by their misfortune.
Lizzie Hexam is a character of profound natural intelligence, dragged down at every turn by the expectations attached to her birth.
The rooftop gives her, momentarily, a life of the mind — and Dickens presents that as not merely pleasant but morally significant.
One notices the detail: Jenny's face is sharper, Lizzie's more perplexed.
That small discrimination tells us everything about the two characters — Jenny's quick mordant intelligence, Lizzie's slower, deeper struggle.
And yet the scene is not without its complications — Dickens introduces it through Fledgeby's gaze, and Fledgeby is not a sympathetic observer.
The carpet, the fruit, the books — Riah has provided all of this.
And that 'old instinct of his race' is a phrase that sits very uneasily in 2024, as it should.
Dickens is trying to be generous to Riah and manages a kind of condescension in the same clause.
The novel's treatment of Riah is one of its genuine tensions — a conscious attempt at repair that does not quite mend what it set out to mend.
That tension is worth its own conversation, and we'll return to it.
But what strikes me, holding all of today's passages together, is that John Harmon is never just a plot mechanism — he is an absence that generates warmth.
The Boffins' grief, Mrs Boffin's adoption impulse, Harmon's own furious gratitude — all of it flows from a man who wasn't supposed to be there.
My thanks to Sir Edmund, Professor Blackstone, and Caroline Woodcourt for a conversation of rare quality.
We'll be back next time to continue our journey through Our Mutual Friend — a novel that never stops surprising.

segments.title: Dickens at Play: Humor, Grotesques, and Comic Mercy

utterances.text: Welcome back to Our Mutual Friend Unpacked.
We've spent time with the novel's darker currents — the river, the dust, the machinery of money.
But Dickens is also, inescapably, one of the great comic writers in the language.
And in this segment we want to ask: what does the humour do?
Is it relief, or is it something more purposeful — mercy, even, extended to characters who might not deserve it?
Caroline Woodcourt is our close reader, and she has been sitting with some of the most delightfully strange comic moments in the book.
Caroline, let's begin with you.
Thank you — and I want to start somewhere that might seem like an odd choice for a segment about humour.
We're in the very first chapter, out on the river at night, and Gaffer Hexam has just pulled something from the water.
And what Dickens does next is almost ritualistically funny — grotesquely, darkly funny.
He finds money on the body, and the prose slows right down to watch him handle it.
'He chinked it once, and he blew upon it once, and he spat upon it once,—"for luck," he hoarsely said—before he put it in his pocket.'
That triple repetition — chinked, blew, spat — it's almost liturgical.
And then 'for luck' — delivered hoarsely, as though he's embarrassed by his own superstition.
It's repulsive and yet you can't help but laugh — and that laughter implicates you immediately.
Caroline puts her finger on something essential there — the comedy of that passage is inseparable from its moral weight.
Dickens is not mocking Gaffer for being poor or for doing what he does.
He is mocking the ceremony — the way human beings will perform respectability around any act, however sordid.
The spitting on coins for luck is a genuine folk custom — and Dickens deploys it to expose the absurdity of luck-seeking in a world governed by death.
Johnson would say the comic here is doing exactly what comedy ought — holding up a mirror and inviting us to see ourselves in the reflection.
And the historical detail is entirely accurate, which sharpens it considerably.
River-finders — those who salvaged from the Thames — were a recognised if deeply marginal profession in mid-Victorian London.
Mayhew documented them in exhaustive detail: the hierarchy, the territories, the protocols.
So when Gaffer ritually blesses the coins taken from a corpse, Dickens is being grimly precise about an actual social practice.
The grotesque comedy isn't exaggeration — it's reportage with a novelist's ear.
That's exactly right — and the comedy gets tenderer, I think, as the novel moves toward its close.
There's a scene near the end with Bella, Mr Boffin, and the baby — and it's one of the most openly joyful passages in all of Dickens.
Bella has just discovered that Boffin's apparent transformation into a miser was entirely a performance, staged to test and correct her.
And her response is glorious — she kneels beside him and she speaks in this breathless, childlike rush.
'Please I don't believe you are a hard-hearted miser at all, and please I don't believe you ever for one single minute were!'
That repeated 'please' — it's not polite, it's urgent, almost frantic with relief.
She's laughing and crying and confessing all at once.
Dickens is at full stretch here — comic, tender, deeply moral — and it lands because the whole novel has been building to this moment.
What strikes me about that scene is how Bella's absurd formality — all those 'pleases' — is itself a kind of moral restitution.
She has spent much of the novel being haughty and acquisitive, and now she prostrates herself — literally, she kneels — in the language of a child asking forgiveness.
Burke would recognise this as a natural form of moral recovery — one cannot re-enter the moral order by argument alone; one must perform it.
And the comedy makes it bearable — even lovable — rather than mawkish.
I'd add that the scene only works because we understand what the Boffins' performance actually cost.
Mr Boffin chose to be thought a miser — one of the most despised figures in Victorian moral taxonomy — in order to save someone else's character.
That is a remarkable act of social self-sacrifice, and the comedy wraps around it like a kind of protective warmth.
Dickens understands that laughter is how people survive the things they cannot say plainly.
And then there's the scene I find almost impossible to read without grinning — the unmasking of the so-called 'ever-wakeful dustman.'
Wegg has been persecuted throughout by this mysterious nocturnal figure — this bandaged, menacing dustman apparition.
And then Dickens simply — almost casually — pulls the curtain back.
'Who, untying his tied-up broken head, revealed a head that was whole, and a face that was Sloppy's.'
Sloppy — this enormous, guileless, endlessly kind creature who can read the newspaper like a performance — has been tormenting the scheming Wegg.
The syntax itself is funny: 'a head that was whole, and a face that was Sloppy's' — two revelations delivered with such deadpan elegance.
Comic justice at its most merciful — the villain undone by the innocent.
Sloppy is one of Dickens's great comic gifts to the novel — and his goodness is never sentimentalised into silliness.
He is simple, yes — but his simplicity is not presented as a deficiency.
It is presented as a form of natural virtue that the clever and acquisitive characters entirely lack.
That is a deeply conservative moral vision, and I mean that as a compliment — the world is not made better by cleverness, but by goodness.
Though we should note that Sloppy's origin — a foundling raised by Betty Higden — places him in the very machinery of the Poor Law that the novel attacks.
He has survived the worst that Victorian institutional charity can inflict, and emerged capable of an elaborate act of justice.
That is not accidental — Dickens is making a pointed argument about where moral resilience actually comes from.
And he wraps it in a comic reveal so light-fingered that you might miss the polemic entirely.
That feels like precisely the right note on which to pause — the comedy and the argument running so closely together you can barely separate them.
From Gaffer's coin ritual on the dark river, to Bella's exultant kneeling, to Sloppy's bandaged face revealed — Dickens is using laughter to do some of his most serious work.
Coming up, we turn to the question of inheritance and identity — what it means to be John Harmon, and whether a man can remake himself by renouncing wealth.

segments.title: Society's Refuse and the Question of Worth

utterances.text: We turn now to the novel's most haunting preoccupation: the question of who, in this society, is considered to have worth — and who is discarded.
Three figures will guide us through this territory: a seven-year-old boy shivering at a fire, a woman who weaves visions out of pain, and a man whose testimony may hang another.
James Blackstone begins — because the child at the centre of this story is also a legal object, a pawn in his father's will, and James understands better than anyone what that meant in practice.

What Boffin gives us in this passage is something quite rare in the novel: a direct, unmediated account of John Harmon as a child — not as a legal estate, not as a missing heir, but as a small boy going to a foreign school alone.
The detail that the old man wouldn't hear of allowing a sixpence coach-money tells you everything about the father's character — and everything about the boy's position in that household.
This is a child who has no claim on comfort — not because the law failed him, but because the law was entirely in his father's hands.
And then Dickens — through Boffin's voice — gives us this:
"There was his little scanty travelling clothes upon him. There was his little scanty box outside in the shivering wind."
That word "scanty" — twice — is doing precise moral work.
It is not poverty described from the outside; it is poverty felt, from the ground up.
And what strikes me — every time I read this — is that Boffin is not a natural prose stylist.
He speaks in rough, warm, tumbling rhythms. And yet when he gets to Mrs Boffin at the fire, the writing becomes almost liturgical.
Listen to the verbs — "stands him by her, kneels down at the fire, warms her two open hands, and falls to rubbing his cheeks."
"She holds him round the neck, like as if she was protecting him, and cries to me, 'I'd give the wide wide world, I would, to run away with him!'"
That repetition — "wide wide world" — is pure ballad, pure folk speech.
It's the grammar of longing. And it costs her nothing to say it and everything not to.
One notices that the boy does not speak much. He has one line — "I must go! God bless you!" — and then he rests his heart against her bosom and looks up.
Dickens tells us that look was "as if it was in pain — in agony."
"Such a look!" — and he leaves it there. Three words. He trusts us.
The novel consistently gives its most inarticulate figures the most articulate suffering — and I think this is rather more than social conscience at work.
It is a recognition that suffering which cannot speak for itself is not thereby diminished — it is, if anything, enlarged.
That enlargement through silence is precisely what makes Jenny Wren so extraordinary — and so difficult for the other characters in the novel to process.
Jenny is a child in pain — chronic, physical pain — and the world around her, frankly, would prefer not to look directly at her.
And yet she constructs from that pain a vision that is, in its own terms, luminous.
She describes children coming to her in long bright slanting rows — not the children of the neighbours, not the children who mocked her — but these:
"'Who is this in pain! Who is this in pain!' When I told them who it was, they answered, 'Come and play with us!'"
She has been excluded from childhood itself — from play, from ease, from the ordinary traffic of being young.
And her imagination restores it — not by pretending the pain away, but by making it the very credential that summons these bright presences.
What undoes me every time is the phrase "made me light."
She says: "They swept about me and took me up, and made me light."
For a girl whose body is her prison — whose every waking hour is organised around pain — to be made light is not metaphor. It is the most precise longing she could name.
And then: "Have patience, and we will come again." That refrain haunts the whole passage.
She has built an entire theology of endurance from this vision — and she offers it to others, freely, without bitterness.
One wants to resist the temptation to sentimentalise Jenny — and she is sentimentalised, occasionally, by critics who read her purely as a figure of innocent suffering.
But the passage insists on her as a knowing, active intelligence.
She says — with that extraordinary aside — "in a tone as though it were ages ago."
This child speaks from the perspective of an ancient — she has been compressed by suffering into something harder and wiser than her years.
She is not sentimental about herself. She is the one character who has the fewest illusions, which makes her visions all the more arresting.
And then we have Riderhood — who sits at the opposite pole of this moral universe entirely.
Where Jenny's testimony is a vision given freely, Riderhood's is a transaction — carefully rehearsed, deployed for legal advantage against Gaffer Hexam.
He prefaces the alleged confession with a remarkable little formula: "precious be the obligations of a Alfred David" — his garbled version of an affidavit, a legal oath.
He is performing legality while almost certainly betraying it.
And the alleged words he puts into Gaffer's mouth are stripped to the bone:
"There was foul play then. I done it for his money. Don't betray me!"
Whether or not Gaffer said those words, the structural irony is devastating — the betrayer is the one crying "Don't betray me."
What I find most chilling about the Riderhood passage is its absolute confidence in its own performance.
He keeps correcting himself — "I think he said in a score, but of that I am not positive, so take the lowest figure."
These little hedges are a kind of theatre of honesty — they're designed to make us trust the rest.
Dickens understands that the most dangerous liars are not the ones who over-claim — they're the ones who ostentatiously under-claim.
The contrast between Jenny and Riderhood is, I think, the novel's sharpest moral geometry.
Both are marginal figures — both are, in the novel's own terms, society's refuse — but one has transformed suffering into vision and the other has transformed it into leverage.
The novel does not moralize the difference. It simply places the two in the reader's hands and trusts us to feel it.
Society's refuse, transfigured — or weaponised. That tension will stay with us through the rest of the episode.
Coming up: we follow the money — and ask what it does to the people who pursue it, and the people who unexpectedly inherit it.
We've spent this episode tracing the moral and social currents that run through Our Mutual Friend — the dust, the money, the masks people wear.
In this final segment, I want to bring us to the question of where Dickens locates hope — what redemption actually looks like in this novel.
It isn't a blaze of light — it tends to arrive quietly, in a shared meal, a confession, an act of trust between two people.
Edmund, I'd like to start with you — because you've been drawn throughout to the moral imagination of individual characters rather than social forces.
Where does Dickens place the real weight of his redemptive vision?
It is, I think, precisely in the privacy of conscience — and nowhere more strikingly than in John Harmon's long, solitary self-examination.
Dickens gives us a man conducting what one can only call a cross-examination of himself — and the verdict he reaches is unflinching.
The passage has this extraordinary rhetorical device — he literally says to himself, 'Now, stop, and so far think it out, John Harmon.'
'I came back, shrinking from my father's money, shrinking from my father's memory, mistrustful of being forced on a mercenary wife.'
The repetition of 'shrinking' is not decoration — it is the precise psychological word for a man recoiling from an inheritance that has never meant anything but misery.
And the self-interrogation culminates in that splendid, quiet affirmation: 'Is that so? That is exactly so.' — which is a kind of moral courage of its own.
This is not a man reformed by society — he is reformed by his own scrupulous honesty with himself.
What strikes me in that passage is how close it comes to breaking down entirely — the rhythm of it is a man steadying himself, almost aloud.
And the tenderness — 'the two dear noble honest friends who had made the only sunlight in my childish life' — that phrase stopped me cold on first reading.
'Knowing of nothing but wretchedness that my father's wealth had ever brought about' — that's the indictment, isn't it.
It's not that money is evil in the abstract — it's that this particular wealth has a history, and the history is one of damage.
What redeems John Harmon isn't renouncing the money — it's choosing Bella freely, on the other side of that knowledge.
And Dickens earns that — I think it's one of the most quietly earned love stories in all Victorian fiction.
I don't disagree with either of you — but I want to hold the personal and the structural together for a moment.
Because the same novel that gives us Harmon's interior redemption also shows us Wegg's entirely unreconstructed greed — and Dickens takes considerable care with that contrast.
Wegg's scheme is laid out with a kind of grotesque bureaucratic precision — and the language Dickens gives him is the language of a man who has fully internalised the market's worst logic.
The proposal is that Boffin should be, and I quote directly —
'kept in a state of abject moral bondage and slavery until the time when they should see fit to permit him to purchase his freedom at the price of half his possessions.'
'Purchase his freedom' — Dickens is very precise there.
The vocabulary of commerce has colonised even the language of liberation — and Wegg, monstrous as he is, is in that sense a perfectly logical product of the world the novel describes.
James is right that Dickens knew his villains — and Wegg is a remarkable creation precisely because he is so thoroughly, comically self-deceived.
But I would argue the structural pressure makes the domestic redemptions more luminous, not less.
Consider the supper scene — Bella, Rokesmith, and old Wilfer in that incongruous little room.
'It was a delicious repast; by far the most delicious that Bella, or John Rokesmith, or even R. Wilfer had ever made.'
The superlative is doing real work there — 'by far the most delicious' — when the meal is plainly modest by any material standard.
Dickens is telling us that sufficiency, freely chosen and shared in love, exceeds every abundance tainted by compulsion or mercenary calculation.
The nursery hobgoblin image is wonderful — it's so disarming, so playful, and yet it carries real weight.
Dickens writes —
'like the supper provided for the three nursery hobgoblins at their house in the forest, without their thunderous low growlings of the alarming discovery, Somebody's been drinking my milk!'
Without the growlings — that's the key.
The fairy tale feast is only menacing when possession and resentment enter — remove those, and what you have left is simply warmth and abundance.
And those two brass knobs of the iron safe staring from the corner like 'the eyes of some dull dragon' — the money world is still present, still watching.
But it doesn't win here. It just stares, dully, at people who have found something it cannot quantify.
And then there is Bradley Headstone — who serves as a kind of dark mirror to all of this.
Because where Harmon undergoes a genuine reckoning with himself and is redeemed, Headstone is trapped in a reckoning that goes nowhere.
The passage describing his state is one of the most frightening pieces of psychological writing in the novel.
'He had no remorse; but the evildoer who can hold that avenger at bay, cannot escape the slower torture of incessantly doing the evil deed again and doing it more efficiently.'
'More efficiently' — that is a devastating detail.
The mind without remorse doesn't rest — it rehearses, it refines, it optimises the original act of destruction.
That is Dickens's answer to the question of what happens when mutual affection is replaced by obsession — the self becomes its own inescapable prison.
The contrast is structurally perfect — and Dickens understood perfectly that punishment without repentance is not liberation but an aggravation.
Headstone's torment is described as 'a state that aggravates the offence by doing the deed a thousand times instead of once' — which is the novel's profoundest moral statement.
Against that, the simple shared meal, the honest self-examination, the freely given love — these are not sentimental consolations.
They are the only genuine alternative Dickens can imagine to a world organised by greed and compulsion.
That feels like exactly the right note on which to close — redemption not as grand reversal, but as something quietly, stubbornly chosen.
Edmund, James, Caroline — it has been a genuine pleasure to think through this novel with you.
Our Mutual Friend remains, I think, one of the most demanding and most rewarding novels in the English language — and this conversation has only deepened that conviction for me.
Thank you for joining us on Our Mutual Friend Unpacked.

There was an innocent piece of dinner-furniture that went upon easy
      castors and was kept over a livery stable-yard in Duke Street, Saint
      James’s, when not in use, to whom the Veneerings were a source of blind
      confusion. The name of this article was Twemlow. Being first cousin to
      Lord Snigsworth, he was in frequent requisition, and at many houses might
      be said to represent the dining-table in its normal state. Mr and Mrs
      Veneering, for example, arranging a dinner, habitually started with
      Twemlow, and then put leaves in him, or added guests to him. Sometimes,
      the table consisted of Twemlow and half a dozen leaves; sometimes, of
      Twemlow and a dozen leaves; sometimes, Twemlow was pulled out to his
      utmost extent of twenty leaves. Mr and Mrs Veneering on occasions of
      ceremony faced each other in the centre of the board, and thus the
      parallel still held; for, it always happened that the more Twemlow was
      pulled out, the further he found himself from the center, and nearer to
      the sideboard at one end of the room, or the window-curtains at the other.
c2:p2.summary: Twemlow, a man of good family connections, is introduced through an extended metaphor comparing him to a dining table that the Veneerings manipulate for social purposes.

c27:p51.text:
The consideration of Mrs Boffin had clothed Mr Sloppy in a suit of black,
      on which the tailor had received personal directions from Rokesmith to
      expend the utmost cunning of his art, with a view to the concealment of
      the cohering and sustaining buttons. But, so much more powerful were the
      frailties of Sloppy’s form than the strongest resources of tailoring
      science, that he now stood before the Council, a perfect Argus in the way
      of buttons: shining and winking and gleaming and twinkling out of a
      hundred of those eyes of bright metal, at the dazzled spectators. The
      artistic taste of some unknown hatter had furnished him with a hatband of
      wholesale capacity which was fluted behind, from the crown of his hat to
      the brim, and terminated in a black bunch, from which the imagination
      shrunk discomfited and the reason revolted. Some special powers with which
      his legs were endowed, had already hitched up his glossy trousers at the
      ankles, and bagged them at the knees; while similar gifts in his arms had
      raised his coat-sleeves from his wrists and accumulated them at his
      elbows. Thus set forth, with the additional embellishments of a very
      little tail to his coat, and a yawning gulf at his waistband, Sloppy stood
      confessed.
c27:p51.summary: Sloppy's new black suit is a comedic disaster: buttons gleam like eyes, the hatband is absurdly fluted, his sleeves ride up and trousers bag at the knees, and his coat has a yawning gap at the waistband.
c27:p51.best_quote: he now stood before the Council, a perfect Argus in the way of buttons: shining and winking and gleaming and twinkling out of a hundred of those eyes of bright metal, at the dazzled spectators.

Then, the train rattled among the house-tops, and among the ragged sides
      of houses torn down to make way for it, and over the swarming streets, and
      under the fruitful earth, until it shot across the river: bursting over
      the quiet surface like a bomb-shell, and gone again as if it had exploded
      in the rush of smoke and steam and glare. A little more, and again it
      roared across the river, a great rocket: spurning the watery turnings and
      doublings with ineffable contempt, and going straight to its end, as
      Father Time goes to his. To whom it is no matter what living waters run
      high or low, reflect the heavenly lights and darknesses, produce their
      little growth of weeds and flowers, turn here, turn there, are noisy or
      still, are troubled or at rest, for their course has one sure termination,
      though their sources and devices are many.

‘But two could play at your game,’ said Riderhood, snapping his fingers at
      him half a dozen times, ‘and I played it long ago; long afore you tried
      your clumsy hand at it; in days when you hadn’t begun croaking your
      lecters or what not in your school. I know to a figure how you done it.
      Where you stole away, I could steal away arter you, and do it knowinger
      than you. I know how you come away from London in your own clothes, and
      where you changed your clothes, and hid your clothes. I see you with my
      own eyes take your own clothes from their hiding-place among them felled
      trees, and take a dip in the river to account for your dressing yourself,
      to any one as might come by. I see you rise up Bradley Headstone, Master,
      where you sat down Bargeman. I see you pitch your Bargeman’s bundle into
      the river. I hooked your Bargeman’s bundle out of the river. I’ve got your
      Bargeman’s clothes, tore this way and that way with the scuffle, stained
      green with the grass, and spattered all over with what bust from the
      blows. I’ve got them, and I’ve got you. I don’t care a curse for the
      T’other governor, alive or dead, but I care a many curses for my own self.
      And as you laid your plots agin me and was a sly devil agin me, I’ll be
      paid for it—I’ll be paid for it—I’ll be paid for it—till
      I’ve drained you dry!’
c65:p84.summary: Riderhood describes in detail how he witnessed Bradley's transformation, possession of the bloody bargeman's suit, and his intent to drain Bradley financially until completely ruined as punishment.

‘Yes; and it’s pleasant to know that you are Mrs Boffin,’ said her
      husband, ‘and it’s been a pleasant thing to know this many and many a
      year!’ It was ruin to Mrs Boffin’s aspirations, but, having so spoken,
      they sat side by side, a hopelessly Unfashionable pair.

‘However, a sociable word or two on these mistakes became an easy
      introduction between us, and the weather was hot, and he helped me to a
      cool cabin on deck alongside his own, and his first school had been at
      Brussels as mine had been, and he had learnt French as I had learnt it,
      and he had a little history of himself to relate—God only knows how
      much of it true, and how much of it false—that had its likeness to
      mine. I had been a seaman too. So we got to be confidential together, and
      the more easily yet, because he and every one on board had known by
      general rumour what I was making the voyage to England for. By such
      degrees and means, he came to the knowledge of my uneasiness of mind, and
      of its setting at that time in the direction of desiring to see and form
      some judgment of my allotted wife, before she could possibly know me for
      myself; also to try Mrs Boffin and give her a glad surprise. So the plot
      was made out of our getting common sailors’ dresses (as he was able to
      guide me about London), and throwing ourselves in Bella Wilfer’s
      neighbourhood, and trying to put ourselves in her way, and doing whatever
      chance might favour on the spot, and seeing what came of it. If nothing
      came of it, I should be no worse off, and there would merely be a short
      delay in my presenting myself to Lightwood. I have all these facts right?
      Yes. They are all accurately right.

‘I have checked the calculation often, and it must have been two nights
      that I lay recovering in that public-house. Let me see. Yes. I am sure it
      was while I lay in that bed there, that the thought entered my head of
      turning the danger I had passed through, to the account of being for some
      time supposed to have disappeared mysteriously, and of proving Bella. The
      dread of our being forced on one another, and perpetuating the fate that
      seemed to have fallen on my father’s riches—the fate that they
      should lead to nothing but evil—was strong upon the moral timidity

‘The child’s father is employed by the house that employs me; that’s how I
      came to know it, Charley. The father is like his own father, a weak
      wretched trembling creature, falling to pieces, never sober. But a good
      workman too, at the work he does. The mother is dead. This poor ailing

‘I don’t. And if  they  do, my dear, they ought to learn better,’ said Mr
      Boffin. ‘Patrons and Patronesses, and Vice-Patrons and Vice-Patronesses,
      and Deceased Patrons and Deceased Patronesses, and Ex-Vice-Patrons and
      Ex-Vice-Patronesses, what does it all mean in the books of the Charities
      that come pouring in on Rokesmith as he sits among ’em pretty well up to
      his neck! If Mr Tom Noakes gives his five shillings ain’t he a Patron, and

Not one other word did Bradley utter all that night. Not once did he
      change his attitude, or loosen his hold upon his wrist. Rigid before the
      fire, as if it were a charmed flame that was turning him old, he sat, with
      the dark lines deepening in his face, its stare becoming more and more
      haggard, its surface turning whiter and whiter as if it were being
      overspread with ashes, and the very texture and colour of his hair
      degenerating.

      letters, what a set is made at the man marked by a stroke of notoriety. Oh

      dust of the Golden Dustman! Fifty-seven churches to be erected with

      and paper. Large fat private double letter, sealed with ducal coronet.

c17:p5.text:
These are the corporate beggars. But there are, besides, the individual
      beggars; and how does the heart of the Secretary fail him when he has to
      cope with  them!  And they must be coped with to some extent, because they
      all enclose documents (they call their scraps documents; but they are, as
      to papers deserving the name, what minced veal is to a calf), the
      non-return of which would be their ruin. That is to say, they are utterly
      ruined now, but they would be more utterly ruined then. Among these
      correspondents are several daughters of general officers, long accustomed
      to every luxury of life (except spelling), who little thought, when their
      gallant fathers waged war in the Peninsula, that they would ever have to
      appeal to those whom Providence, in its inscrutable wisdom, has blessed
      with untold gold, and from among whom they select the name of Nicodemus
      Boffin, Esquire, for a maiden effort in this wise, understanding that he
      has such a heart as never was. The Secretary learns, too, that confidence
      between man and wife would seem to obtain but rarely when virtue is in
      distress, so numerous are the wives who take up their pens to ask Mr
      Boffin for money without the knowledge of their devoted husbands, who
      would never permit it; while, on the other hand, so numerous are the
      husbands who take up their pens to ask Mr Boffin for money without the
      knowledge of their devoted wives, who would instantly go out of their
      senses if they had the least suspicion of the circumstance. There are the
      inspired beggars, too. These were sitting, only yesterday evening, musing
      over a fragment of candle which must soon go out and leave them in the
      dark for the rest of their nights, when surely some Angel whispered the
      name of Nicodemus Boffin, Esquire, to their souls, imparting rays of hope,
      nay confidence, to which they had long been strangers! Akin to these are
      the suggestively-befriended beggars. They were partaking of a cold potato
      and water by the flickering and gloomy light of a lucifer-match, in their
      lodgings (rent considerably in arrear, and heartless landlady threatening
      expulsion ‘like a dog’ into the streets), when a gifted friend happening
      to look in, said, ‘Write immediately to Nicodemus Boffin, Esquire,’ and
      would take no denial. There are the nobly independent beggars too. These,
      in the days of their abundance, ever regarded gold as dross, and have not
      yet got over that only impediment in the way of their amassing wealth, but
      they want no dross from Nicodemus Boffin, Esquire; No, Mr Boffin; the
      world may term it pride, paltry pride if you will, but they wouldn’t take
      it if you offered it; a loan, sir—for fourteen weeks to the day,
      interest calculated at the rate of five per cent per annum, to be bestowed
      upon any charitable institution you may name—is all they want of
      you, and if you have the meanness to refuse it, count on being despised by
      these great spirits. There are the beggars of punctual business-habits
      too. These will make an end of themselves at a quarter to one P.M. on
      Tuesday, if no Post-office order is in the interim received from Nicodemus
      Boffin, Esquire; arriving after a quarter to one P.M. on Tuesday, it need
      not be sent, as they will then (having made an exact memorandum of the
      heartless circumstances) be ‘cold in death.’ There are the beggars on
      horseback too, in another sense from the sense of the proverb. These are
      mounted and ready to start on the highway to affluence. The goal is before
      them, the road is in the best condition, their spurs are on, the steed is
      willing, but, at the last moment, for want of some special thing—a
      clock, a violin, an astronomical telescope, an electrifying machine—they
      must dismount for ever, unless they receive its equivalent in money from
      Nicodemus Boffin, Esquire. Less given to detail are the beggars who make
      sporting ventures. These, usually to be addressed in reply under initials
      at a country post-office, inquire in feminine hands, Dare one who cannot
      disclose herself to Nicodemus Boffin, Esquire, but whose name might
      startle him were it revealed, solicit the immediate advance of two hundred
      pounds from unexpected riches exercising their noblest privilege in the
      trust of a common humanity?
c17:p5.summary: The Secretary catalogs individual beggars seeking Boffin's charity—daughters of officers, distressed wives and husbands, those claiming divine inspiration, independent beggars offering loans, and those threatening suicide—each category satirically anatomized.

‘And speaking of satisfactory,’ pursued Mr Boffin, ‘why, Lord save us!
      when we come to take it to pieces, bit by bit, where’s the
      satisfactoriness of the money as yet? When the old man does right the poor
      boy after all, the poor boy gets no good of it. He gets made away with, at
      the moment when he’s lifting (as one may say) the cup and sarser to his
      lips. Mr Lightwood, I will now name to you, that on behalf of the poor
      dear boy, me and Mrs Boffin have stood out against the old man times out
      of number, till he has called us every name he could lay his tongue to. I
      have seen him, after Mrs Boffin has given him her mind respecting the
      claims of the nat’ral affections, catch off Mrs Boffin’s bonnet (she wore,
      in general, a black straw, perched as a matter of convenience on the top
      of her head), and send it spinning across the yard. I have indeed. And
      once, when he did this in a manner that amounted to personal, I should
      have given him a rattler for himself, if Mrs Boffin hadn’t thrown herself
      betwixt us, and received flush on the temple. Which dropped her, Mr
      Lightwood. Dropped her.’

c64:p101.text:
‘Now, scoundrel,’ he pursued, ‘I am going to finish. You supposed me just
      now, to be the possessor of my father’s property.—So I am. But
      through any act of my father’s, or by any right I have? No. Through the
      munificence of Mr Boffin. The conditions that he made with me, before
      parting with the secret of the Dutch bottle, were, that I should take the
      fortune, and that he should take his Mound and no more. I owe everything I
      possess, solely to the disinterestedness, uprightness, tenderness,
      goodness (there are no words to satisfy me) of Mr and Mrs Boffin. And
      when, knowing what I knew, I saw such a mud-worm as you presume to rise in
      this house against this noble soul, the wonder is,’ added John Harmon
      through his clenched teeth, and with a very ugly turn indeed on Wegg’s
      cravat, ‘that I didn’t try to twist your head off, and fling  that  out of
      window! So. That’s the last short speech, do you understand?’

c67:p57.text:
When I devised this story, I foresaw the likelihood that a class of
      readers and commentators would suppose that I was at great pains to
      conceal exactly what I was at great pains to suggest: namely, that Mr John
      Harmon was not slain, and that Mr John Rokesmith was he. Pleasing myself
      with the idea that the supposition might in part arise out of some
      ingenuity in the story, and thinking it worth while, in the interests of
      art, to hint to an audience that an artist (of whatever denomination) may
      perhaps be trusted to know what he is about in his vocation, if they will
      concede him a little patience, I was not alarmed by the anticipation.

Mrs Boffin pulled his nearest ear, in acknowledgment of this piece of
      philosophy, and then said, gradually toning down to a motherly strain:
      ‘Last, and not least, I have taken a fancy. You remember dear little John

‘John dear,’ said Bella, ‘you’re a good nurse; will you please hold baby?’
      Having deposited the Inexhaustible in his arms with those words, Bella
      looked hard at Mr Boffin, who had moved to a table where he was leaning
      his head upon his hand with his face turned away, and, quietly settling
      herself on her knees at his side, and drawing one arm over his shoulder,
      said: ‘Please I beg your pardon, and I made a small mistake of a word when
      I took leave of you last. Please I think you are better (not worse) than

      Blackberry Jones, better (not worse) than any of them! Please something

      him and forced him to turn his delighted face to hers. ‘Please I have
      found out something not yet mentioned. Please I don’t believe you are a
      hard-hearted miser at all, and please I don’t believe you ever for one

c8:p43.text:
‘The last time me and Mrs Boffin saw the poor boy,’ said Mr Boffin,
      warming (as fat usually does) with a tendency to melt, ‘he was a child of
      seven year old. For when he came back to make intercession for his sister,
      me and Mrs Boffin were away overlooking a country contract which was to be
      sifted before carted, and he was come and gone in a single hour. I say he
      was a child of seven year old. He was going away, all alone and forlorn,
      to that foreign school, and he come into our place, situate up the yard of
      the present Bower, to have a warm at our fire. There was his little scanty
      travelling clothes upon him. There was his little scanty box outside in
      the shivering wind, which I was going to carry for him down to the
      steamboat, as the old man wouldn’t hear of allowing a sixpence
      coach-money. Mrs Boffin, then quite a young woman and pictur of a
      full-blown rose, stands him by her, kneels down at the fire, warms her two
      open hands, and falls to rubbing his cheeks; but seeing the tears come
      into the child’s eyes, the tears come fast into her own, and she holds him
      round the neck, like as if she was protecting him, and cries to me, “I’d
      give the wide wide world, I would, to run away with him!” I don’t say but
      what it cut me, and but what it at the same time heightened my feelings of
      admiration for Mrs Boffin. The poor child clings to her for awhile, as she
      clings to him, and then, when the old man calls, he says “I must go! God
      bless you!” and for a moment rests his heart against her bosom, and looks
      up at both of us, as if it was in pain—in agony. Such a look! I went
      aboard with him (I gave him first what little treat I thought he’d like),
      and I left him when he had fallen asleep in his berth, and I came back to
      Mrs Boffin. But tell her what I would of how I had left him, it all went
      for nothing, for, according to her thoughts, he never changed that look
      that he had looked up at us two. But it did one piece of good. Mrs Boffin
      and me had no child of our own, and had sometimes wished that how we had
      one. But not now. “We might both of us die,” says Mrs Boffin, “and other
      eyes might see that lonely look in our child.” So of a night, when it was
      very cold, or when the wind roared, or the rain dripped heavy, she would
      wake sobbing, and call out in a fluster, “Don’t you see the poor child’s
      face? O shelter the poor child!”—till in course of years it gently
      wore out, as many things do.’

c19:p76.text:
‘I dare say my birds sing better than other birds, and my flowers smell
      better than other flowers. For when I was a little child,’ in a tone as
      though it were ages ago, ‘the children that I used to see early in the
      morning were very different from any others that I ever saw. They were not
      like me; they were not chilled, anxious, ragged, or beaten; they were
      never in pain. They were not like the children of the neighbours; they
      never made me tremble all over, by setting up shrill noises, and they
      never mocked me. Such numbers of them too! All in white dresses, and with
      something shining on the borders, and on their heads, that I have never
      been able to imitate with my work, though I know it so well. They used to
      come down in long bright slanting rows, and say all together, “Who is this
      in pain! Who is this in pain!” When I told them who it was, they answered,
      “Come and play with us!” When I said “I never play! I can’t play!” they
      swept about me and took me up, and made me light. Then it was all
      delicious ease and rest till they laid me down, and said, all together,
      “Have patience, and we will come again.” Whenever they came back, I used
      to know they were coming before I saw the long bright rows, by hearing
      them ask, all together a long way off, “Who is this in pain! Who is this
      in pain!” And I used to cry out, “O my blessed children, it’s poor me.
      Have pity on me. Take me up and make me light!”’

‘’Scuse  me , Lawyer Lightwood, it’s a part of the truth, and as such I do

      my boat.” I says to him, “Gaffer, I know it.” He says to me, “Rogue
      Riderhood, you are a man in a dozen”—I think he said in a score, but
      of that I am not positive, so take the lowest figure, for precious be the
      obligations of a Alfred David. “And,” he says, “when your fellow-men is
      up, be it their lives or be it their watches, sharp is ever the word with

c30:p7.text:
‘When I came to England, attracted to the country with which I had none
      but most miserable associations, by the accounts of my fine inheritance
      that found me abroad, I came back, shrinking from my father’s money,
      shrinking from my father’s memory, mistrustful of being forced on a
      mercenary wife, mistrustful of my father’s intention in thrusting that
      marriage on me, mistrustful that I was already growing avaricious,
      mistrustful that I was slackening in gratitude to the two dear noble
      honest friends who had made the only sunlight in my childish life or that
      of my heartbroken sister. I came back, timid, divided in my mind, afraid
      of myself and everybody here, knowing of nothing but wretchedness that my
      father’s wealth had ever brought about. Now, stop, and so far think it
      out, John Harmon. Is that so? That is exactly so.
c30:p7.summary: John Harmon explains that he returned to England reluctantly, conflicted about his inherited wealth, fearful of a mercenary marriage, and anxious about his own character.

c40:p72.text:
On this head, Silas Wegg had much to say. Silas had to say That, he would
      beg to remind his comrade, brother, and partner, of the impressive
      passages they had read that evening; of the evident parallel in Mr
      Boffin’s mind between them and the late owner of the Bower, and the
      present circumstances of the Bower; of the bottle; and of the box. That,
      the fortunes of his brother and comrade, and of himself were evidently
      made, inasmuch as they had but to put their price upon this document, and
      get that price from the minion of fortune and the worm of the hour: who
      now appeared to be less of a minion and more of a worm than had been
      previously supposed. That, he considered it plain that such price was
      stateable in a single expressive word, and that the word was, ‘Halves!’
      That, the question then arose when ‘Halves!’ should be called. That, here
      he had a plan of action to recommend, with a conditional clause. That, the
      plan of action was that they should lie by with patience; that, they
      should allow the Mounds to be gradually levelled and cleared away, while
      retaining to themselves their present opportunity of watching the process—which
      would be, he conceived, to put the trouble and cost of daily digging and
      delving upon somebody else, while they might nightly turn such complete
      disturbance of the dust to the account of their own private investigations—and
      that, when the Mounds were gone, and they had worked those chances for
      their own joint benefit solely, they should then, and not before, explode
      on the minion and worm. But here came the conditional clause, and to this
      he entreated the special attention of his comrade, brother, and partner.
      It was not to be borne that the minion and worm should carry off any of
      that property which was now to be regarded as their own property. When he,
      Mr Wegg, had seen the minion surreptitiously making off with that bottle,
      and its precious contents unknown, he had looked upon him in the light of
      a mere robber, and, as such, would have despoiled him of his ill-gotten
      gain, but for the judicious interference of his comrade, brother, and
      partner. Therefore, the conditional clause he proposed was, that, if the
      minion should return in his late sneaking manner, and if, being closely
      watched, he should be found to possess himself of anything, no matter
      what, the sharp sword impending over his head should be instantly shown
      him, he should be strictly examined as to what he knew or suspected,
      should be severely handled by them his masters, and should be kept in a
      state of abject moral bondage and slavery until the time when they should
      see fit to permit him to purchase his freedom at the price of half his
      possessions. If, said Mr Wegg by way of peroration, he had erred in saying
      only ‘Halves!’ he trusted to his comrade, brother, and partner not to
      hesitate to set him right, and to reprove his weakness. It might be more
      according to the rights of things, to say Two-thirds; it might be more
      according to the rights of things, to say Three-fourths. On those points
      he was ever open to correction.

If Boffin is caught secretly removing anything, they will interrogate and enslave him morally until he pays for his freedom.

It was, as Bella gaily said, like the supper provided for the three
      nursery hobgoblins at their house in the forest, without their thunderous
      low growlings of the alarming discovery, ‘Somebody’s been drinking  my 
      milk!’ It was a delicious repast; by far the most delicious that Bella, or
      John Rokesmith, or even R. Wilfer had ever made. The uncongenial oddity of
      its surroundings, with the two brass knobs of the iron safe of Chicksey,
      Veneering, and Stobbles staring from a corner, like the eyes of some dull
      dragon, only made it the more delightful.
c49:p79.summary: The narrator poetically describes their simple meal as surpassing all previous experience—like the fairy tale feast of the three hobgoblins, but without threat or discord.

c57:p53.text:
Now, too, was he cursed with a state of mind more wearing and more
      wearisome than remorse. He had no remorse; but the evildoer who can hold
      that avenger at bay, cannot escape the slower torture of incessantly doing
      the evil deed again and doing it more efficiently. In the defensive
      declarations and pretended confessions of murderers, the pursuing shadow
      of this torture may be traced through every lie they tell. If I had done
      it as alleged, is it conceivable that I would have made this and this
      mistake? If I had done it as alleged, should I have left that unguarded
      place which that false and wicked witness against me so infamously deposed
      to? The state of that wretch who continually finds the weak spots in his
      own crime, and strives to strengthen them when it is unchangeable, is a
      state that aggravates the offence by doing the deed a thousand times
      instead of once; but it is a state, too, that tauntingly visits the
      offence upon a sullen unrepentant nature with its heaviest punishment
      every time.
c57:p53.summary: The narrator explores the psychological torment of murderers without remorse: they are compelled to endlessly re-enact and mentally perfect their crime, creating a torture worse than remorse itself.
